newsitem.title: ISRAEL: PLO sees Hebron pact by Tuesday -- lawmakers.
newsitem.headline: PLO sees Hebron pact by Tuesday -- lawmakers.

text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat expects that a long-overdue deal for handing over the town of Hebron to PLO self-rule will be signed with Israel at the end of the month, Palestinian legislators said on Thursday.
East Jerusalem lawmaker Ziyad Abu Ziyad told Reuters that Arafat announced the dates while briefing Palestinian lawmakers in Ramallah on progress in talks with Israel on the Hebron deal.

"If the Israelis go ahead with their promises and the plans which were planned maybe it will be possible to conclude an agreement on the 30th and the 31st (of December)," Abu Ziyad said after the meeting with Arafat.
The remarks, confirmed by other lawmakers, reinforced the forecast of a senior Israeli official who told reporters on Tuesday night he expected a deal by the end of the year.

But Abu Ziyad added Arafat was cautious: "President Arafat said that maybe there would be no agreement at all...this (Israeli) government has been cunning and maneuvering and trying to run away and ignore their commitments."

A summit on Tuesday between Arafat and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ended weeks of deadlock in talks on Israel's long overdue handover of 80 percent of Hebron to the Palestinians in the Israeli-occupied West Bank.

While negotiators for the two sides met at a Jerusalem hotel to iron out the details in the U.S.-brokered talks, tensions remained high in the West Bank town itself. A firebomb was thrown beside a Jewish enclave but caused no injuries or damage.
Netanyahu wants security guarantees for the 400 Israeli settlers in the heart of the town of 100,000 Arabs which is sacred to both Moslems and Jews.

"I would expect there will be another meeting between the two leaders when the agreement is ready," Edward Abington, U.S. Consul General for East Jerusalem, told reporters on Thursday. "I don't expect that will be very long."

Most of Netanyahu's 18 cabinet members are expected to back the deal but some in the cabinet, including hawkish former general Ariel Sharon, have openly criticised the deal as dangerous for the Jews of Hebron.

Hebron, taken by Israel with the rest of the West Bank in the 1967 Middle East war, is the last Palestinian town due for self-rule under a 1995 peace deal. Israel's security fears have delayed its transfer.

The pullout from Hebron is seen as key to any further Israeli-PLO peace moves. Arabs view the pullout -- promised by Israel's former government -- as an acid test of Netanyahu's intentions toward the Middle East peace process as a whole.

U.S. Middle East envoy Dennis Ross headed home overnight to brief President Bill Clinton on the talks which had been deadlocked since October. He said he would be back on Monday to seal the agreement.

In the Gaza Strip, Israel opened a road to Palestinians closed two years ago near the Jewish settlement of Netzarim that had been closed since the killing of three soldiers by an Islamist suicide bomber on a bicycle in November 1994.

"It coincides with the general reconciliatory atmosphere," said Brigadier-General Saeb al-Ajez, Palestinian police commander in the northern strip, who took part in the reopening with an Israeli commander.
The fate of the Jews in Gaza, Hebron and other West Bank settlements will be decided in "final-status" talks between Israel and the Palestinians due to be completed by May 1999.
